title: India brings back tax-free imports of small polished diamonds for exporters
subtitle: From 20 Nov 2026, big diamond exporters can again import tiny natural stones without paying IGST, if they export more value within six months.
content_html:
Picture a diamond that weighs less than a quarter of a carat, a stone you could lose on a tablecloth. India now lets some big exporters bring stones like that into the country without paying tax at the border. On Friday, 20 November 2026, the finance ministry issued a notification that brings back a tax break on imports of small cut and polished diamonds. The relief started the same day, 20 November.

The break works under a plan called the Diamond Imprest Authorisation, or DIA for short. The plan covers IGST, basic customs duty and some other import charges. For India's diamond makers, this is about cash in hand.

First, what is IGST?

IGST means Integrated Goods and Services Tax. In India, goods brought in from abroad are treated like goods moving from one state to another, so IGST is charged on imports, on top of basic customs duty. Customs duty is simply a tax paid when goods enter the country.

Here is the catch. A business can usually claim this IGST back later, as a credit against the firm's own tax bill. But the firm still has to pay the money first. Think of a school trip where every student pays Rs 500 upfront and gets it back only after the trip. The money comes home in the end, but for weeks it is stuck. A tax adviser's guide puts it simply: such charges raise working capital costs.

Working capital is the day to day money a business needs to buy material, pay workers and keep running. When tax eats into it, a diamond firm has less cash for the next batch of stones.

Why does India import polished diamonds at all?

It sounds odd. Why buy a diamond that is already polished? Under the DIA plan, a firm brings in small polished stones, works on them and sends them out again worth more than before. The plan is also meant to keep this work in India, so that firms do not move to diamond-mining countries that want stones cut locally.

This trade is huge in Gujarat. Surat is known as the Diamond City of India, and about 90% of the world's diamonds are cut and polished in Surat, says Wikipedia. So any change to the cost of moving diamonds in and out of India lands first on Surat's polishing units.

What changed on 20 November?

The DIA plan began in January 2025. The Economic Times says the aim was to help Indian diamond exporters, especially small firms, at a time when their exports were falling. The plan started working on 1 April 2025.

Then came a twist. A policy change in 2025 took away the exemption on IGST and compensation cess, while other duty exemptions stayed. An exemption is a rule that says you do not have to pay a tax. Compensation cess is an extra charge whose money was used to make up for shortfalls in states' GST income.

The new notification brings the IGST exemption back. The Economic Times calls it a reversal of last year's change.

Who gets the break?

Not every jeweller in the bazaar. The rules are strict. To qualify, an exporter must hold at least two-star export house status. That is a status the government gives to firms based on how much they have exported. The exporter must also have sold at least $15 million worth of diamonds abroad in each of the last three financial years, and must have filed their tax returns.

There is also a limit on how much one firm may bring in. Imports are capped at 5% of the firm's average yearly export of cut and polished diamonds over the last three financial years, and never more than $15 million.

Here is a simple example to see how the cap works. Say a firm exports diamonds worth $100 million a year on average. Five percent of that is $5 million, so that is its limit. A much bigger firm exporting $400 million a year would get 5% as $20 million, but the cap stops it at $15 million.

Which diamonds count?

Only natural diamonds. The plan covers semi-processed, half-cut and broken natural diamonds too, but lab-grown and synthetic diamonds are left out. Each stone can weigh no more than 25 cents. In diamond talk, 100 cents make one carat, so 25 cents is a quarter of a carat. That is tiny.

What must the exporter do in return?

The tax break is not a free gift. The plan is a deal, a bit like a library book: you can borrow it free, but you must return it on time. The notification says the importer must export within six months of customs clearance, with at least 10% value addition, paid in foreign currency.

Value addition means the goods must be worth more when they leave than when they came in. So if a firm imports diamonds worth $1 million, it must export cut and polished diamonds worth at least $1.1 million. The amount exported also cannot be less than the amount imported.

There are more rules. All imports and exports under the plan must go through Mumbai airport, with customs clearance at the Precious Cargo Customs Clearance Centre at the Bharat Diamond Bourse. The firm must use the stones itself and cannot sell them on to anyone else, even after meeting the export promise. It must also give a bond and security equal to the tax it did not pay. A bond is a written promise backed by money that the government can keep if the firm breaks the rules.

What does this mean for money and work?

For eligible diamond firms, the big change is cash. They no longer have to pay IGST upfront on these small stones and wait to get the money back. That money can stay in the business for the next batch of work.

The Economic Times notes that the plan was made to help exporters when they were facing falling exports and job losses. Each firm's tax-free imports are tied to what the firm has already exported, so the benefit goes to firms that keep shipping diamonds abroad.

The big picture

A tax that is paid now and returned later still ties up money while it waits, as the tax adviser's guide above notes. By bringing back the IGST exemption from 20 November 2026, the government has made it cheaper for qualifying exporters to keep tiny diamonds moving through Indian workshops and back out to the world.
